questions.stem: As the temperature of an intrinsic semiconductor is raised, its conductivity

options.text: increases, because more electrons are excited across the band gap
stays constant, because the gap is fixed
falls to zero at the melting point

questions.explanation: A small rise in temperature frees many more electrons from the valence band into the conduction band (and creates equally many holes). Carrier density soars, so resistivity falls and conductivity rises. In a metal the carrier density is already huge; heating mainly increases lattice vibrations, so metallic conductivity falls.

distractorRationale.a: That is the metallic pattern. Semiconductors do the opposite, which is a standard WAEC discriminator
distractorRationale.c: The gap size is roughly constant, but the number of electrons able to cross it is not — it grows exponentially with T
distractorRationale.d: Melting is irrelevant here; conductivity of a semiconductor is already rising well below the melting point

questions.stem: The essential distinction among conductors, semiconductors and insulators is the

options.text: size of the energy gap between valence and conduction bands
number of neutrons in each nucleus

questions.explanation: Band theory classifies solids by the gap. Overlap or a partly filled band means a conductor; a small gap means a semiconductor; a large gap means an insulator. Density, nuclear composition and melting point do not decide whether electrons can reach a conduction band.

distractorRationale.a: Lead is denser than silicon but is a conductor for a different reason: its bands overlap
distractorRationale.c: Neutron number identifies isotopes; it does not set electrical conduction
distractorRationale.d: Tungsten melts at a very high temperature and is still a metal; diamond is an insulator with a high melting point too

questions.stem: Doping silicon with phosphorus produces

options.text: p-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers
n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
an insulator, because phosphorus fills the gap
a conductor with overlapping bands like copper

questions.explanation: Phosphorus is pentavalent (a donor). Four electrons bond to silicon; the fifth is easily freed, so extra negative carriers appear. The material is n-type. It is still a semiconductor — doping raises carrier density by orders of magnitude, but it does not turn silicon into a metal.

distractorRationale.a: Holes as majority carriers come from a trivalent acceptor such as boron, not from phosphorus
distractorRationale.c: Donors add carriers; they do not widen the gap into an insulator
distractorRationale.d: Doped silicon remains a semiconductor with a band gap; it does not acquire the overlapping bands of copper

questions.stem: Boron is used as an acceptor impurity in silicon because it is

options.text: pentavalent, and so donates a free electron
trivalent, and so creates a hole in the bonding structure
divalent, and so forms an ionic bond with silicon
hexavalent, and so fills the conduction band

questions.explanation: Boron is in group III (trivalent). It has only three outer electrons with which to bond to four neighbouring silicon atoms, so one bond is incomplete — a hole, which can move as a positive majority carrier. That is p-type doping.

distractorRationale.a: Pentavalent donors (P, As, Sb) produce n-type material, not p-type
distractorRationale.c: Boron is not divalent here; semiconductor doping is a covalent-crystal story, not an ionic salt
distractorRationale.d: Boron is not hexavalent, and doping does not 'fill the conduction band' in that sense

questions.stem: A p–n junction diode is forward-biased when

options.text: the p-side is connected to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive
the p-side is connected to the positive terminal and the n-side to the negative
both sides are connected to the positive terminal
no external battery is used, so the depletion layer vanishes

questions.explanation: Forward bias drives holes from the p-side and electrons from the n-side toward the junction, thinning the depletion layer and lowering the barrier so a large current can flow. Conventionally that means p to +, n to −, in the direction of the diode-symbol arrow.

distractorRationale.a: That is reverse bias: the depletion layer widens and current is almost zero
distractorRationale.c: Both terminals at the same polarity is not a defined bias; there is no complete circuit through the junction
distractorRationale.d: With no battery the depletion layer is still there; that is the unbiased junction with its built-in barrier

questions.stem: In half-wave rectification of a.c., the number of diodes required in the simplest circuit is

options.text: 0, because a resistor already converts a.c. to d.c.

questions.explanation: A single diode in series with the load passes one half-cycle and blocks the other — half-wave rectification. Two diodes are used with a centre-tap transformer for full-wave; four diodes make a bridge full-wave rectifier. A resistor cannot rectify: it does not have a one-way characteristic.

distractorRationale.b: Two diodes appear in the centre-tap full-wave circuit, not in the simplest half-wave circuit
distractorRationale.c: Four diodes form a bridge full-wave rectifier
distractorRationale.d: A resistor obeys Ohm's law in both directions; it cannot convert a.c. to d.c.

questions.stem: Compared with a half-wave rectifier, a full-wave bridge rectifier supplying the same a.c. source and load

options.text: uses only the positive half-cycles and wastes the negative ones
produces a pulsing d.c. output at twice the supply frequency, using both half-cycles
converts a.c. into perfectly smooth d.c. with no further components
blocks both half-cycles, so the load current is zero

questions.explanation: In a bridge, one pair of diodes conducts on the positive half-cycle and the other pair on the negative half-cycle, always sending current through the load in the same direction. Both halves are used, so the pulse frequency is $2f$. The output is still pulsing; a capacitor filter is needed if smooth d.c. is wanted.

distractorRationale.a: That describes half-wave rectification, which throws away every other half-cycle
distractorRationale.c: Bridge output is unidirectional but still rippled; smoothing is a separate step
distractorRationale.d: That would be an open circuit, not a rectifier

questions.stem: Which statement about doped semiconductors is correct?

options.text: n-type material has a net negative charge because of the extra electrons
p-type material has a net positive charge because of the holes
both n-type and p-type crystals are electrically neutral overall
doping replaces silicon atoms with copper atoms so that the crystal becomes a metal

questions.explanation: Each donor or acceptor atom is electrically neutral when it is added. In n-type, the extra free electron is balanced by the extra proton in the donor nucleus. In p-type, the hole is balanced by one fewer proton in the acceptor nucleus. Majority-carrier sign is not the same thing as a net charge on the sample. Copper would not be a dopant in this sense; it would wreck the covalent lattice rather than create a controlled n- or p-type semiconductor.

distractorRationale.a: Extra free electrons are offset by extra nuclear charge on the donor atoms; the crystal is not charged
distractorRationale.b: Holes are offset by the smaller nuclear charge of the acceptor; p-type is not a positively charged object
distractorRationale.d: Doping uses group III or group V atoms in tiny concentration; it does not turn silicon into copper

distractorRationale.c: While temperature affects conductivity, intrinsic refers specifically to purity.
distractorRationale.d: Excess holes indicate doping or external influences, not intrinsic properties.
